title: Transactional email: What it is and how it works
content:
Transactional emails are automated messages triggered by a specific action a customer takes, sent to help that person complete or follow up on something already in progress. An order receipt, a password reset confirmation, or a shipping notification are all examples of transactional emails because each one delivers information tied to an action the recipient just took.
That’s what sets transactional email apart from marketing email: a promotional campaign persuades a broad audience to take a new action, like making a purchase, while a transactional email responds to an action that’s already happened, delivering information the recipient needs rather than trying to sell them something.
Because transactional emails are expected, timely, and directly relevant to the recipient, they tend to see higher open rates than marketing emails. But that reliability only holds when they’re set up correctly: triggered at the right moment, formatted clearly, and compliant with email regulations.
This guide breaks down what transactional emails are, how they work behind the scenes, and how to set them up across the customer journey from order confirmations to renewal reminders. It also covers compliance essentials and how to monitor transactional email performance.
A transactional email is a one-to-one operational message triggered by a specific user action or system event. Some examples of transactional emails are:
The email system sends each transactional message to one recipient because something relevant happened to that person or account. “One-to-one” describes that event-to-recipient relationship; however, emails can still be generated automatically at scale.
Transactional emails shouldn’t be confused with bulk emails, where the sender chooses a segment and distributes substantially similar content according to a campaign schedule.
Marketing email creates demand or prompts a new commercial action. Transactional email helps users complete, confirm, or monitor an interaction already underway. Automation and personalization can apply to both. However, the sending infrastructure for marketing and transactional emails has to be separated.
A marketing campaign can cause volume spikes, complaints, or bounces. Shared infrastructure between marketing and transactional email can let those problems linger or filter password resets, receipts, and account alerts. For this reason, it’s not uncommon for large email sender platforms like Yahoo to recommend separating marketing and transactional traffic by IP address or DKIM domain.
Separation also protects customer trust. A marketing opt-out can stop promotions without suppressing essential transactional notifications. Customers also learn that operational emails will lead with the information they need, rather than hide it beneath a sales pitch.
Featured resource: The Difference Between Marketing Email and Transactional Email
The strongest transactional email examples solve one immediate customer need. They confirm access, document a payment, report progress, or surface relevant account activity. Let’s walk through real-world examples of transactional emails at each stage of the customer lifecycle, organized by type.
Account and security emails protect access from signup onward. Common examples include password resets, login alerts, and two-factor authentication codes. Each message should identify the event, explain the next step, and state when a link or code expires. Login alerts should also show the device, time, or approximate location. That context helps users separate a legitimate warning from phishing.
For example, HubSpot nudges all their users to protect their accounts with two-factor authentication.
Reddit’s password reset is another example of account and security notification emails. Not only does Reddit make a user follow the link to reset their password, but the company also advises what to do in case the user didn’t make that request.
Order, billing, and renewal emails reduce support tickets because customers don’t need to hunt through an account portal to find this information. An order confirmation records what the customer bought and what happens next. A receipt proves payment, while a failed-payment notice helps prevent service interruption.
Hospital Medicover informs patients about their paid appointments and how to prepare for the procedure.
Renewal emails are sent before the anniversary purchase date in case a user wants to cancel the subscription. Unfortunately, not all companies send renewal emails, but those that do typically include the plan name, renewal date, charge amount, and cancellation route.
Formula 1 TV, a paid monthly streaming service, lays out its renewal and cancellation terms right in your first purchase confirmation email.
Shipping and service update emails cover what happens after a customer buys something. They typically include tracking updates, delay alerts, and support confirmations that keep customers informed about order status and help requests. Every message should answer three questions:
Climbing equipment company Clevo provides a great example of shipping update emails. In one email, Clevo provides an order tracking link, the shipping status, and the receipt and contact information should any issues occur.
Rossmann, a retail company selling household and baby essentials, exceeded my expectations in handling order issues. Apparently, Rossmann had trouble syncing its warehouse inventory with its online store, because I ended up paying for a few items that were actually out of stock.
To resolve the issue, Rossmann sent an automatic email informing me of my incomplete order and the steps I could take: keep the rest of the order with a partial refund or cancel it altogether. Rossmann’s automatic email is a brilliant way to kill two birds with one stone: keep the customer happy while cutting costs by keeping a support agent out of the loop.
Task assignments, mentions, review requests, and community digests keep users current without requiring constant app checks. These messages qualify as transactional notifications when they report activity tied to the recipient’s account or preferences.
Digests need extra care. Product promotions can shift their purpose toward email marketing , so account activity should remain the main content. For mixed messages, the FTC’s CAN-SPAM guidance tells U.S. senders to examine the subject line and content order. Promotional framing can make the entire email commercial. Asana’s task mention is the simplest example of transactional email in this category.
A connected CRM setup makes sure each transactional email uses the right customer record, the right template, and a clear send history. Below, we’ll cover an example of how HubSpot’s transactional emails connect CRM data, tracking, and API sending paths. With that setup, marketers will own the message while developers control the product event that triggers it.
Start by defining the exact event that should send the email.
For example, a receipt should receive an email only after a payment is confirmed as successful. Before the email goes out, make sure the payment processor confirms the charge. After that, an integration should send required details, such as the amount, currency, receipt ID, and timestamp. This helps prevent emails from being sent for failed or incomplete events. Next, decide which system owns each piece of data:
Single-Send associates each email with a contact and creates one when no match exists. SMTP API can make contact creation optional. Choose SMTP API when your own application renders the email or when creating a CRM contact would add noise.
Pro tip: Evaluate any transactional email API service against three facts: event owner, template owner, and contact-creation rule. That decision prevents fragile integrations and months of CRM cleanup.
Use a workflow when HubSpot is the system that should decide when the email is sent. HubSpot workflows can handle branching, delays, record updates, and email actions in the same automation. For example, you can branch by language, plan, or region before sending the message.
Before launching, test the workflow with a real record. HubSpot’s workflow test tool lets you preview how a record would move through the flow without actually executing the actions. When you test, the path is shown in the workflow preview so you can spot logic mistakes before going live.
Note: For time-sensitive emails, such as password resets or receipts, a direct API path is often better. That reduces delay and keeps the application in control of the send.
First, build the transactional email in HubSpot and keep it focused on the specific event, such as a receipt, password reset, or invoice update. Next, add the key details the email needs, such as the customer name, receipt number, amount paid, or reset link. If a personalization token has no value , it can appear blank, so check important fields carefully before sending. Then, test both the message and the automation:
Finally, use HubSpot’s version history to track changes to the workflow over time, and revert to a prior version if needed — note that reverts aren’t supported for workflows containing webhook or custom code actions. Keep API schemas and integration code in source control with each release tied to a named template version. This helps you trace changes, reproduce issues, and roll back safely when a deployment breaks email rendering or event processing.
Sinch Mailgun’s 2026 research analyzed more than 400 billion emails and found that nearly 18% failed to reach the inbox . For transactional messages, that failure can block account access, delay revenue, or generate avoidable support cases. Let’s look into the non-negotiable technical and operational steps that keep transactional emails out of spam folders and off blocklists.
Set up SPF, DKIM, and DMARC before sending production traffic.
Gmail requires SPF or DKIM from all senders. Senders exceeding 5,000 Gmail messages daily need SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. Gmail also requires TLS, valid forward and reverse DNS, and RFC 5322 formatting .
After publishing the records, send test messages to Gmail and Outlook. Gmail’s “Show original” view should report PASS for SPF, DKIM, and DMARC.
Review DMARC reports to identify forgotten tools or unauthorized senders. Repeat this check whenever you add new email sending services. One missing provider can break authentication for an otherwise healthy domain.
Send transactional notifications through a separate authenticated subdomain, “From” address, and delivery stream. High-volume programs should also consider a separate IP pool and queue. Gmail recommends different IP addresses for account notifications and promotional messages. Marketers who use HubSpot for transactional email sends can configure a dedicated IP reserved for transactional traffic right inside the ecosystem and start using it immediately.
Configure your transactional email platform to return a status event for every message. These events tell you where the email succeeded or failed. Record each event against the same message ID so support can trace the email from trigger to outcome.
Amazon Simple Email Service, or Amazon SES , is one platform that provides these events. It is an AWS cloud service that any company can connect to its website or application. It has no connection to selling products on Amazon or using Fulfillment by Amazon.
Use HubSpot’s delivery records and reporting if your company already sends through HubSpot.
In Sinch’s 2025 survey of 3,180 shoppers, 75% expected order confirmations within five minutes . Speed gets the message into the customer’s hands. Clear design helps get the key message across at a glance.
The subject line should identify the event and its status: “Payment received,” “Password reset requested,” or “Order confirmed.” Avoid sensitive account details in the subject.
I like when transactional emails specify the sender in the subject line. It helps me recognize valuable emails in my cluttered inbox instantly.
Inside the email, put the status, amount or date, next step, and support route above the fold. Give the customer one primary action. Secondary links should never compete with tracking an order or securing an account.
Build accessibility into the template before adding branding. In HubSpot’s drag-and-drop email builder , start with a responsive, single-column layout. Place the status, essential details, primary action, and support link in reading order. HubSpot’s templates are responsive by default , and the editor lets you control how modules stack on mobile.
HubSpot’s image modules also include fields for adding alt text . These controls help marketers create an accessible foundation without editing HTML. You still need to write descriptive button labels, avoid color-only status indicators, and maintain 4.5:1 contrast for normal text .
A light cross-sell can fit after a completed, low-risk transaction. Keep it related to what the customer already bought and place it below all operational details. The subject line, preview text, and primary button should remain transactional . Gmail’s current sender guidance tells teams not to mix promotional content into sales receipt messages , so marketers need to be extremely careful if they plan to do so.
Definitely skip promotions in password resets, login alerts, failed-payment notices, refunds, and service incidents.
Every marketer needs to know and understand legal and regulatory requirements that apply to transactional emails.
Do transactional emails need an unsubscribe link? In the U.S., a message that fits the FTC’s narrow definition of transactional or relationship email generally does not need an unsubscribe link, although its routing information must remain truthful.
The UK ICO similarly excludes purely administrative service messages from direct marketing, but adding promotional content can change that , so you’ll have to add an opt-out link.
Write a subject line that states the customer event, such as “Payment received” or “Your renewal date changed.” Under FTC guidance , a mixed-purpose email may be treated as commercial when its subject line promotes an offer or its transactional content does not appear mainly at the beginning. Put the status, amount or date, required action, and support route first in the email template. Keep the sender name, Reply-To address, and routing details accurate as well.
Be careful in what information you log. Don’t retain reset links, security codes, or full payment information since GDPR requires companies to delete it once it no longer serves a documented purpose. Plus, there’s a huge risk that exposed logs could give a hacker account access or sensitive financial data.
Log only the message ID, recipient, trigger, template version, send time, and delivery result.
Transactional email deliverability is healthy when messages arrive quickly, reach the inbox, and help recipients complete the expected action. Measure each email type separately because a delayed password reset is more urgent than a delayed order confirmation.
For each transactional email type, track delivery, inboxing signals, and task completion.
A hard bounce signals a permanent failure, so suppress that address instead of sending again. Complaints show that recipients consider the message unwanted, while blocks often point to authentication, reputation, or content problems. Review these metrics by message type and mailbox provider to identify where the failure occurs.
Delivery, latency, and retry metrics show whether transactional emails leave your system fast and what stops them when they don’t. Find these events in your provider’s delivery logs.
Transactional emails don’t need an unsubscribe link when the email is strictly necessary to complete or manage a requested service, such as a receipt or security alert. The U.S. and EU generally apply unsubscribe requirements to marketing rather than purely operational messages. However, definitions and exemptions vary by jurisdiction, especially under Canada’s CASL. Review the message’s purpose, content, and recipient market before removing the link.
Yes, sometimes you can include promotions in a transactional email carefully. The promotion must not overtake the operational purpose. Under FTC guidance , a promotional subject line or marketing content placed before the transaction details can make the email commercial. UK guidance is stricter: promotional content may turn a service message into direct marketing. For global sends, keep cross-sells in a separate marketing email .
Not automatically. A dedicated IP isolates transactional email reputation, but it needs steady sending volume and proper warm-up. Amazon SES recommends shared IPs for low or irregular volume and dedicated IPs for larger, predictable programs. Choose based on sending patterns.
First , store a message ID, trigger, recipient, template version, timestamps, and final status for every send. When an email fails, confirm that the trigger fired, required data reached the template, and the provider accepted the request.
Second , read the error event: retry temporary delays, suppress permanent bounces, and fix authentication or rendering errors before resending. Amazon SES event logs and HubSpot’s Single-Send API status show the type of send history a provider should expose.
There are two ways to define this: from the customer’s standpoint and from a technical one.
Customers never see your email stack. They see whether the password reset arrives, or whether the receipt lists the correct amount. That level of accuracy can’t happen without a robust technical setup working behind the scenes.
The best transactional email service connects the two: accurate CRM data, controlled templates, protected sending infrastructure, and searchable delivery logs, all working together so the customer-facing result stays reliable.
That’s where HubSpot’s email marketing software becomes indispensable. It keeps customer data, automation, and technical settings in one system, so marketers can control the email experience while developers control the trigger. The result is fewer handoffs and more satisfied customers.

title: SERPs Stop Being The Default Between 2028 & 2030 via @sejournal, @DuaneForrester
content:
The ranked results page stops being Google’s default first response for most queries somewhere between 2028 and 2030, starting in the U.S., with the UK and EU following a year or more behind. That is my forecast, not a finding, and the rest of this piece separates the two as carefully as I can. By “stops being the default” I mean something specific. The SERP does not get deleted. It gets demoted to one step away, a place you can still reach on purpose but no longer the place you land by default.
Disclosure up front: my company measures AI visibility and data, so a world with less SERP is not neutral ground for me. In my 2027 predictions piece , I argued the ranked page would persist through next year as a legacy interface while the consequential decisions moved elsewhere, and last week , I walked through the research that would let Google rank without an index at all. This piece is about the clock rather than the mechanism: when the page stops being where people land.
If you have read much vendor content since May, you may believe that already happened. A widely repeated claim says Google made AI Mode the global default at I/O 2026. Google’s own announcement says something narrower: Gemini 3.5 Flash became “the new default model in AI Mode for everyone globally,” the search box got its biggest rebuild in 25 years , and “you’ll continue to get a range of results from Search, just like you do today.” Two weeks later, when a Chrome Canary flag briefly sent address-bar searches straight into AI Mode, Google’s VP of Search Engineering Rajan Patel called it an error and wrote, “We’re not planning to make AI Mode the default for Chrome searches.” The default has not flipped. Yet.
In May 2024, Google launched a “Web” filter that shows only text-based links, sitting alongside Images, Videos, and News or tucked under More. Danny Sullivan announced it as a convenience for people who prefer plain links. Read two years later, it looks like infrastructure. The filter already does what a demoted SERP needs: it presents ranked links as one view among several, reachable with a click or a URL parameter, and promoting the answer layer above it requires no new engineering.
That changes the question. Google does not need to build anything to move the ranked list one step away. It needs a reason to change which view loads first, so the forecast is really about when the reasons line up.
Start with the answer layer’s share of the page. In Pew Research Center’s browsing study of 900 U.S. adults in March 2025, 18% of Google searches produced an AI summary, and users clicked a traditional result in 8% of visits with a summary against 15% without one. By May 2026, Similarweb’s 2026 Generative AI Landscape put AI Overviews on 43% of US searches, up from 15% a year earlier. Those two measurements use different methods and should not be stitched into one tidy line, but they point in the same direction at roughly the same speed: from under a fifth of U.S. searches to over two-fifths in about 14 months. As an amicus brief in the DOJ appeal noted, no industry-standard measurement of AI Overview prevalence exists, which is why I am relying on direction across sources rather than any single percentage.
Then the conversational layer. Google says AI Mode passed one billion monthly users within a year of launch, with queries “more than doubling every quarter.” Those are Google’s figures, and they are large. Set them beside Similarweb panel data analyzed for a June 2026 zero-click study, which found AI Mode accounted for 0.34% of Google searches from January through April 2026, and the gap shows how this transition actually works. A billion people have tried the answer-first surface, and almost none of them have made it the place they start. Similarweb also measured AI Mode generating outbound referrals on 1.6% to 2.5% of queries, against 17% to 19% for traditional search, which is the clearest single picture of what a default flip would mean for anyone who depends on the click.
Behavior is drifting in the expected direction. Similarweb recorded a 5.4% increase in average Google query length after AI Mode arrived, and longer queries are the ones most likely to trigger a generated answer, so users are gradually phrasing their way into the answer layer. Outside Google, OpenAI reported 900 million weekly ChatGPT users in February 2026, yet Similarweb found most ChatGPT users kept using Google too. The pattern is addition rather than migration, which tells you the SERP is unlikely to lose its default position to a rival. If it loses that position, it loses it to Google itself.
Google has every capability it needs to flip the default tomorrow. It hasn’t, and the reason is money. The ranked page still carries the most proven ad inventory in the history of advertising, while the answer layer’s ad formats are months old. At Google Marketing Live in May, Google introduced ads placed inside AI Mode responses, including formats where Gemini builds the ad around the user’s question, and Google’s own GML recap states, “We aren’t just bringing ads to AI Search experiences; we are reinventing what an ad is in that context.” I described this kind of query-time, auto-generated ad system in August 2025 in Cohorts, Clusters, and the Coming AI Ad System , and it is now arriving in pieces.
The economics on the other side are moving quickly. In his Q2 2026 earnings remarks , Sundar Pichai said Google had “reduced the cost of AI Mode responses to its lowest level since launch” and had “brought together AI Overviews and AI Mode into one seamless Search experience.” Cost to serve is falling, the two surfaces are merging, and the new ad units are maturing. In the same quarter, Network advertising declined 1% . That is the revenue Google earns on other people’s pages, so the part of its business that depends on sending people to the open web is already the part that is shrinking.
Put those together and the trigger becomes visible. Google flips the default when ad yield per query in the answer layer reaches rough parity with the ranked page. Before that point, flipping costs Google money. After it, keeping the old default costs Google money. Everything else in this forecast concerns when that crossover lands and what slows it down.
A quick check on the fastest possible version: if AI Mode’s 0.34% share kept doubling every quarter, it would pass 40% in about seven quarters, which lands in late 2027. Nothing doubles forever, and that share is a panel estimate rather than a count, so late 2027 is the floor the math allows, not a prediction. Its main use is showing that the front edge of my range is not conservative for its own sake.
Three regulatory processes now bear directly on whether a ranked layer stays visible, and they run on different clocks.
In the UK, the Competition and Markets Authority issued binding conduct requirements on June 3, 2026, letting publishers opt out of AI Overviews and AI Mode without being penalized in standard search results, and giving Google nine months to implement them. That puts the deadline around March 2027. Once the rules are in place, a ranked layer in the UK is no longer just a product choice. It is where opted-out publishers are entitled to remain visible, and burying it would invite exactly the scrutiny the rule was written to create.
In the EU, the European Commission opened a formal investigation in December 2025 into whether AI Overviews and AI Mode use publisher content without compensation or a way to refuse without losing access to Google Search. That case is still open, and EU competition cases rarely close quickly.
In the U.S., the Justice Department and the plaintiff states filed their cross-appeal in July 2026, arguing that Judge Mehta should have considered banning Google’s payments to distributors and warning that “a competitive window may close” if Google keeps using search profits against generative AI challengers. The fastest way to flip the default is the address bar in Chrome and Android, which is precisely the distribution the appeal concerns. Google’s statement that it is not planning to make AI Mode the Chrome default can be interpreted differently with that appeal pending.
None of these brakes stops the transition. What they do is make it uneven. A U.S. flip that happens while UK and EU rules are still settling produces a staggered sequence by market, which is why my range starts with the U.S. and puts Europe a year or more behind.
“Extinction” is really three separate events, and treating them as one is how most predictions on this topic go wrong. The first threshold is when a generated answer leads on most queries. The second is the default flip, when the ranked list moves behind a click for most queries on Google’s main surfaces. The third is the long tail, when the remaining query classes where links still lead , such as navigational, local, and some commerce, follow along. In the U.S., the first threshold is close and plausibly crosses half of searches in late 2026 or 2027. The second is the event this piece is dating. The third runs well beyond it.
For a sense of how long Google takes to move between stages like these, the best precedent is mobile-first indexing. Google started it in November 2016, announced in March 2020 that it would move the whole web over, and declared it complete in October 2023. That is roughly three and a half to four years to the default switch, and seven to the end of the tail.
Map that onto the current transition. AI Overviews launched broadly in the US in May 2024, and three and a half to four years from that start lands between late 2027 and mid-2028, which happens to agree with the doubling floor above. AI Mode’s own clock, starting from its U.S. rollout in May 2025, lands in late 2028 or 2029. Mobile-first was a backend change Google controlled almost entirely, with no advertisers to bring along and no regulators watching the outcome. This transition has both, so I am placing the U.S. default flip between 2028 and 2030, with the long tail finishing in the early 2030s.
I think a forecast that cannot fail is not worth publishing, so here are the signals that would move the range.
It comes earlier if Google reverses its position on the Chrome or Android address bar, if AI Mode’s measured share of searches passes roughly 10% in independent panel data, or if Google begins reporting answer-layer ad revenue as its own line, which it would only do once the number looks good.
It comes later, or not at all in this form, if AI Mode’s share plateaus in the low single digits through 2027, if advertisers report weak returns from AI Mode placements once those formats are out of testing, or if the appeals court extends remedies to generative AI distribution in ways that constrain default placement.
None of these signals will arrive cleanly. Most of what practitioners see will be panel estimates, vendor claims, and Google’s own selectively disclosed figures, and separating them is the problem I spend most of my time on at CitationIQ. Whatever tools you use, check these signals quarterly rather than reacting to whatever number is circulating that week.
Here is the forecast in one place. The ranked results page stops being Google’s default first response for most US queries between 2028 and 2030, triggered when answer-layer ad yield reaches parity with the SERP, slowed by UK, EU, and U.S. regulatory processes, and leaving ranked links one click away rather than gone. The harder question is what being indexed is worth once the ranked list is no longer the product.
This post was originally published on Duane Forrester Decodes .
